flawed_step: 0015 (lines 0013-0016: the appeal to [[Intersection with Normal Subgroup is Normal]] to conclude $H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1$, and symmetrically $H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_2$ at line 0016; these are reused as the justifications at lines 0035 and 0038)
counterexample: Take $G = S_3$ with $e$ the identity. Set $H_1 = S_3$, $H_2 = \{e, (1\,2)\}$, $N_1 = A_3 = \{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$, $N_2 = \{e, (1\,2)\}$. All hypotheses of the theorem hold: $N_1 = A_3 \lhd S_3 = H_1$ (index 2), and $N_2 = H_2 \lhd H_2$ (a group is normal in itself). Now $H_1 \cap N_2 = S_3 \cap \{e,(1\,2)\} = \{e,(1\,2)\}$. This is NOT normal in $H_1 = S_3$: conjugating by $(1\,3) \in H_1$ gives $(1\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3)^{-1} = (2\,3) \notin \{e,(1\,2)\}$. So line 0015 is false. (Symmetrically, swapping the roles — $H_1 = \{e,(1\,2)\} = N_1$, $H_2 = S_3$, $N_2 = A_3$ — gives $H_2 \cap N_1 = \{e,(1\,2)\}$ not normal in $H_2 = S_3$, refuting line 0016.) The cited result [[Intersection with Normal Subgroup is Normal]] requires the normal subgroup to be normal in the ambient group $G$ ($N \lhd G$, $H \le G$ $\Rightarrow$ $H \cap N \lhd H$); here only $N_2 \lhd H_2$ and $N_1 \lhd H_1$ are given, and $N_2$ need not be normal in $G$ or in $H_1$, so the hypothesis is not met and the conclusion genuinely fails. Concretely in the first instance, the conjugation identity the proof asserts at line 0035 in the form $x (H_1 \cap N_2) = (H_1 \cap N_2) x$ for all $x \in H_1$ fails at $x = (1\,3)$: $(1\,3)\{e,(1\,2)\} = \{(1\,3),(1\,3)(1\,2)\} = \{(1\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$ while $\{e,(1\,2)\}(1\,3) = \{(1\,3),(1\,2)(1\,3)\} = \{(1\,3),(1\,2\,3)\}$, and these two sets are different.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0011 are fine: $x_h \in H_1 \cap H_2$ gives $x_h \in H_1$ and $x_h \in H_2$, and the stated goal (conjugation-invariance of the product set) is the right target modulo the unstated fact that the product must first be shown to be a subgroup, which the Normal Subgroup Test presupposes. The first step I am certain fails is 0015/0016: the proof invokes [[Intersection with Normal Subgroup is Normal]], whose hypothesis is $N \lhd G$, but the theorem only supplies $N_2 \lhd H_2$ and $N_1 \lhd H_1$. The derived claims $H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1$ and $H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_2$ are not merely unjustified, they are false in general (witness: $G = S_3$, $H_1 = S_3$, $H_2 = N_2 = \{e,(1\,2)\}$, $N_1 = A_3$, where $H_1 \cap N_2 = \{e,(1\,2)\}$ is not normal in $S_3$). These false claims are exactly the justifications cited at lines 0035 and 0038 to move $x_h$ past $H_1 \cap N_2$ and to absorb the conjugation of $H_2 \cap N_1$; as stated, the normality is asserted for all of $H_1$ resp. $H_2$, not just for elements of $H_1 \cap H_2$. The algebra in 0021-0033 is a vacuous insert-and-cancel of $x_h^{-1} x_h$ and is harmless. The error is repairable: since $N_2 \le H_2$ one has $H_1 \cap N_2 = (H_1 \cap H_2) \cap N_2 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2$, and likewise $H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2$, which is all that is needed for $x_h \in H_1 \cap H_2$; the proof would also need the separate observation that $(H_1 \cap N_2)(H_2 \cap N_1)$ is a subgroup (it is, because $H_2 \cap N_1$ is normalised by $H_1 \cap N_2 \le H_1 \cap H_2$). But as written the proof asserts and relies on a false lemma instance, so it is not correct.
